piezas.titulo: Bliki: Generated Glossary
piezas.resumenOriginal: When we use LLMs in a specialized domain, such as the operations of any reasonably-large organization, there is a lot of specialized vocabulary. Such words and specialized meanings will be foreign to an LLM because they aren't in its training set, making it harder for the LLM to be effective when doing tasks in that domain. One technique to aid this is to use an LLM to generate a glossary of the terminology in that domain, and make this glossary available for any LLMs doing work in those circumstances. The sources for the LLM can be any material within the organization concerned such as documents, emails, and chat logs. In some cases getting transcripts of audio or video may be helpful, although most organizations generate enough text to do the job. The glossary-generating LLM should look for single words, and phrases of several words that regularly hang out together to form a meaningful term. The generator should be asked to identify terms that are new to it, but also known terms that are being used in unfamiliar ways. The latter can often cause the most confusion. Once we have a list of specialized vocabulary we can ask the agent to produce a glossary, with definitions for each term. Some terms may be used in different ways, in which case the LLM should provide alternative definitions, with a note as to what context the differences appear in. The LLM can be asked to follow the output format of a dictionary, with a focus on precision and conciseness. Once we have a draft glossary, then human experts in that domain should review it, and amend it for cases where the LLM has got the wrong ends of sticks. We then put the glossary somewhere where any other LLM can use it. It should be in a form that's easy for the LLM to consult, and minimize the tokens the LLM should consume in order to find meaning. We should set up a schedule to review and refresh the glossary at regular intervals, by agents and humans. We should keep it in version control, so we can see how it changes over time. Large organizations often have subtly different definitions in different places, essentially following the Domain Driven Design notion of Bounded Context . Source code can be a particularly interesting bounded context, allowing folks to understand how terminology is used within a code base. Sometimes a single glossary can span several of bounded contexts, but at other times it's better to have separate glossaries for each one, allowing LLMs to consult whichever glossaries that are relevant to what they are doing. I'd urge everyone to resist any temptation to create a single, standard, glossary - I've yet to see that work. Often the value of a glossary isn't to nail down a single definition of a term, but instead to highlight its different usage in different contexts. When there are different bounded contexts it can be interesting to compare different glossaries, or to get LLMs to compare glossaries and describe differences in usage. Comparing a source-code derived glossary to a human text can be particularly instructive. If the glossary is large, it can be worthwhile to only include the terms and links to definitions as part of the initial context. The model can then use the links for only the full definitions it needs while working. A glossary can be used in several ways within Agentic Engineering . Glossaries can inform generation of code, so that names within the generated software fit the particular vocabulary of the enterprise. Sensors in a harness can check for this usage, both in the internals of the software and in the user-interface. When generating code or documents, we may introduce new bounded contexts. For example, internal names that may be used within an organization should not be exposed in a customer-facing UI, because such internal terms are likely to be only confuse a customer. In this case a customer has a different bounded context to the part of the enterprise serving them. It's often useful for glossaries to include terms that should not be used, in which case it includes advice on what other term to use instead. Terms that are deprecated can be handled in this way, with glossary entries that indicate what period of time a term should be in effect. In my conversations with people working with agents in large organizations, a common theme is the difficulty of specialized language. This encourages the activities of domain modeling, building ontologies, and constructing explicit context layers in enterprise data . Getting LLMs to generate a glossary is a simple, but useful, part of this work. piezas.titulo: Transcriptional and DNA Methylation Changes in the Hippocampus and Prefrontal Cortex after Fractionated Cranial Radiation in Mice
piezas.resumenOriginal: Fractionated whole-brain irradiation is essential for treating brain tumors, but many long-term survivors develop cognitive decline whose molecular basis is poorly understood. We asked which cell types and gene programs change late after irradiation, how the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex compare, and whether DNA methylation changes affect the same genes or programs. Male and female mice received whole-brain irradiation (5 x 4 Gy) or anesthesia alone. Irradiated mice showed persistent deficits in executive function and spatial memory. Eleven weeks after irradiation, single-nucleus RNA sequencing and whole-genome bisulfite sequencing of pooled hippocampal (CA1-3) and prefrontal tissue showed cell-type-specific transcriptional changes in neurons of both regions. Both regions showed reduced ribosomal-protein gene expression and changes in adhesion genes, with reduced respiratory-chain genes in prefrontal neurons and bidirectional synaptic gene changes in hippocampus. Differentially methylated regions were enriched at promoters, with hypermethylation predominating in three of the four sex-by-region contrasts. Methylation and gene expression changes pointed to overlapping synaptic and signaling programs, largely through different genes.

piezas.titulo: The role of the right temporal lobe in neural network mechanisms during working memory encoding
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundVisual working memory (vWM) impairment is common in patients with temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) and is more severe in those with right TLE (RTLE), suggesting the significant role of right temporal lobe in WM processes.MethodsWe recruited patients with left TLE (LTLE group, n = 20), RTLE (RTLE group, n = 20) and 35 healthy controls (Control), and examined their vWM performance while simultaneously recording task-based EEG. The alterations in the neural oscillations and neural network were analyzed during the WM encoding phase. In addition, we examined the relationship between the neural oscillations and WM performance, as well as the relationship between the neural network and WM performance, to further explore the role of the right temporal lobe in WM encoding.ResultsRemarkably lower accuracy (both p < 0.001) and significantly longer response times (LTLE vs. Control: p = 0.026; RTLE vs. Control: p < 0.001) were found in both LTLE and RTLE groups compared with controls. The RTLE group experienced notably delayed response time in comparison to the LTLE group (p = 0.026). In comparison to the LTLE group, the RTLE group displayed reduced theta power spectral density for the frontal (p = 0.024) and occipital (p = 0.011) regions, along with the Fz channel (p = 0.047). DTFF_outflow and DTFFz_outflow values in the RTLE group displayed reduction relative to the LTLE group (DTFF_outflow:p = 0.026; DTFFz_outflow: p = 0.037). The LTLE group showed weakened information flow from Fz to P3 (IFFz → P3, ANOVA, F = 3.45, p = 0.037; LSD, LTLE vs. Control: p = 0.013), whereas the RTLE group exhibited weakened information flow from Fz to P4 (IFFz → P4; ANOVA, F = 3.78, p = 0.028; LSD, RTLE vs. Control: p = 0.029), Fz to T4 (IFFz → T4; ANOVA, F = 4.67, p = 0.012; LSD, RTLE vs. Control: p = 0.009), and Fz to TP8 (IFFz → TP8; ANOVA, F = 3.11, p = 0.050; LSD, RTLE vs. Control: p = 0.017), which were positively associated with accuracy and inversely associated with response time.ConclusionAbnormal information transfer from the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex to the superior parietal lobe during the encoding phase may causes WM deficits; damage to information transfer from the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex to the right middle temporal and right inferior temporal gyri exacerbates WM impairments.

piezas.titulo: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video
piezas.resumenOriginal: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works. The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention . Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...] The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units. Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself , allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster. We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues , where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments. piezas.titulo: AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security
piezas.resumenOriginal: This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast . Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance. However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof? There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP? Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution. Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust. How quickly can de-authentication attacks occur? An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system. There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals? Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform. Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration. The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents. Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability. Does true zero-trust architecture exist? The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist? Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub , we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system. We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. Additionally, trust in services is presented by ensuring constraints around their service models where agentic activities are tracked and managed via logs including management of their token revocation list to avoid replay attacks depending on the type of application. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. Things like balancing the adversarial accuracy along with certified adversarial robustness can help to determine how much the model can be trusted. But the question is, can we settle for anything less than foolproof when it comes to deployment of agents in the real world? piezas.resumenOriginal: This retrospective observational study aimed to evaluate the regulatory effects of sensory integration (SI)- based interventions on sensory processing patterns in children aged 7 to 36 months without diagnosed developmental disorders. The intervention group (n = 30) received individualized sensory integration support for at least 6 weeks, while the control group (n = 30) did not receive any specialized support. All participants were assessed using the Sensory Profile (7-36 months). The intervention group showed significantly higher mean scores across all 4 sensory processing quadrants-Low Registration, Sensation Seeking, Sensory Sensitivity, and Sensation Avoiding-compared to the control group ( P < .001). These results suggest that early SI support enhances environmental awareness, behavioral regulation, and modulation of sensory thresholds, even in asymptomatic children. Sensory integration interventions may provide protective and regulatory benefits beyond clinical indications. Findings support the inclusion of sensory screening in early developmental monitoring and the integration of preventive SI strategies in pediatric care models.

piezas.titulo: Validity and Reliability of the Activity Card Sort 3 in Persons With Thumb Carpometacarpal Osteoarthritis.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceAlthough individuals with thumb carpometacarpal (CMC1) osteoarthritis (OA) commonly experience participation restrictions, participation-focused outcome measures remain underinvestigated, and clinicians primarily rely on assessments of impairments in body structures and functions.ObjectiveTo determine the concurrent validity, test-retest reliability, and precision of the Activity Card Sort 3 (ACS3) in individuals with nonoperative CMC1 OA.DesignSingle-cohort observational psychometric study with repeated measures over a 2-week interval.SettingRemote assessments conducted via videoconferencing.ParticipantsThirty-three adults with radiographically confirmed CMC1 OA completed two virtual assessments approximately 2 weeks apart.Outcomes and MeasuresConcurrent validity was examined by comparing ACS3 domain and total scores with the World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0 (WHODAS 2.0). Test-retest reliability of the "current," "previous," and "% retained" activities scores was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC 3,1 ). Precision was assessed using the standard error of measurement and minimal detectable change.ResultsThe ACS3 demonstrated good concurrent validity through strong associations with conceptually related WHODAS 2.0 domains. "Current" and "% retained" scores demonstrated good-to-excellent test-retest reliability across all domains. "Current" scores consistently showed the highest reliability and precision. "Previous" scores demonstrated lower reliability and greater measurement error, suggesting recall bias. Carrying forward "previous" scores from session 1 to session 2 improved the reliability of "% retained" scores.Conclusions and RelevanceThe ACS3 is a valid and reliable measure of participation for individuals with nonoperative CMC1 OA. The "current" and "% retained" scores may support occupational therapy practitioners in conducting participation-focused assessment of persons with CMC1 OA.

piezas.titulo: A spatially continuous cell-type atlas reveals multiscale organization of the human cortex
piezas.resumenOriginal: Neuroimaging has increasingly revealed fine-grained spatial heterogeneity within the human cortex, uncovering regional differentiation beyond conventional cortical divisions. However, understanding the cellular architecture underlying these imaging features requires spatially continuous cell-type references that capture both cortex-wide organization and regional specialization. Here, we introduce RIDGE (Regional Integration of Deconvolution with Guided Estimation), a deconvolution framework that anchors multiple regional references to continuous cortex-wide transcriptomic maps, thereby recovering cortex-wide organizational patterns while supporting region-specific cell-type inference. RIDGE reconstructs spatially continuous distributions of 24 major cortical cell types across the human cortex. The resulting maps are robust across analytical pipelines and independent reference datasets, recover established cell-type associations with known cortical features, and recapitulate the canonical primary sensory-allocortical/periallocortical (Pr-Al) axis of cortical cellular organization. At finer scales, RIDGE resolves distinct cellular profiles across default mode, motor, and visual systems, revealing local cellular specialization within each system. By relating these cellular maps to cortical imaging features, we demonstrate their utility for investigating cellular contributions to global cortical organization and regional specialization. Together, RIDGE provides a unified framework and spatially continuous cellular reference resource for integrating cellular architecture with human cortical imaging across spatial scales.

piezas.titulo: Increased functional connectivity in glioma: separating compensation from tumor-promoting remodeling
piezas.resumenOriginal: Increased functional connectivity (FC) in glioma is often interpreted as compensatory neuroplasticity or tumor-promoting circuit remodeling, although FC is a measure of coupling rather than a mechanism. We propose a qualitative framework that first examines whether the measurement is suitable for the claim, then evaluates evidence for patient function and tumor behavior separately. The two lines of evidence are combined only when they concern the same patient context, anatomical compartment, metric, and time course. The framework also distinguishes maladaptive or excitability-related remodeling from tumor promotion. Human longitudinal studies associate network restoration with recovery, whereas experimental cancer neuroscience shows that neural activity and neuron-glioma synapses can promote malignant behavior. Increased FC should therefore be reported with its modality, metric, comparator, compartment, disease phase, reliability, and prespecified outcomes before being interpreted as compensatory, maladaptive, or tumor-promoting.

piezas.titulo: How Top-Down Are We? Reconsidering the Gap Between Occupational Therapy's Identity and Practice.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Occupational therapy has spent more than a century defining occupation as its professional core. Yet studies across countries and settings show a recurring gap. Therapists value occupation-centered practice while often relying on impairment-focused assessment and intervention. This article argues that the profession may face a translation problem more than an identity problem. Biomedical service structures, standardized measurement, workplace culture, and professional socialization can pull reasoning toward body functions. Bottom-up methods are not inherently incompatible with occupational therapy; the problem arises when change in a component is treated as sufficient evidence of occupational success. Drawing on occupational therapy research, the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, rehabilitation science, and disability rights, we argue that occupation and participation should remain the outcomes that organize assessment, intervention, and evaluation. Practical changes are proposed for clinical reasoning, outcome measurement, education, supervision, and service design.
